extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film industry observers, and media/ethics researchers interested in film promotion practices
extracted.subtask_short: film advertising ethics and quote usage
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes standards, practices, and ethical issues around the use of critics' quotations in film advertising, illustrated by the David Manning hoax and related Sony practices. Useful for understanding what is permitted, common practices, and potential legal/consumer consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPA approval requirement for advertisement campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisement campaigns must be approved by the Motion Picture Association (MPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although campaigns require MPA approval, the article notes that "the MPA does not check quotations on advertisements for their accuracy," so approval does not equal factual verification. Example: ad campaigns for studio releases still go through MPA approval even when quoted material has been edited or fabricated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and honest representation of critics' quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations used in advertising should accurately represent critics' words and context (ethical standard for film promotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that studios are given leeway and often shorten or remove context to put positive spin on quotes. It also presents the anti-pattern of fabrication: marketing executives have been quoted saying they will 'make it up' if a sound bite doesn't exist. The David Manning case (a pseudonymous/fictitious critic credited to a real local paper) illustrates deceptive misuse of quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/avoidance of fabricating critics or attributing false endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent critics, pseudonyms, or attribute quotes to people/newspapers that did not produce them; fabricating reviewer identities is deceptive and unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The David Manning example: a pseudonym used by a Sony marketing executive produced consistently good reviews and was credited to The Ridgefield Press though the paper had never heard of him. Such practices raise ethics questions and can lead to reputational damage and legal scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted editorial practices: shortening or removing context for brevity/positive spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios commonly shorten quotes or remove context in advertising to keep material brief and emphasize positive language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes this as a widespread practice — studios 'may shorten quotes or remove context from them, both to keep things brief and to put as much positive spin as possible.' This is presented as a common tactic rather than a legal prohibition, but it intersects with ethical concerns when context removal misleads consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential legal/consumer remedies for misleading advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading promotional practices can lead to legal claims and consumer remediation (e.g., settlements and refunds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sony's out-of-court settlement on August 3, 2005, agreeing to refund $5 each to dissatisfied customers who saw certain films as a result of Manning's reviews. The article links such outcomes to controversies over ethics in film promotion.
